weightSource.text: Mark/percentage breakdown per syllabus section, per the RCPsych Paper B blueprint (confirmed against an independent published guide, not just the syllabus PDF, which does not itself print a marks table).

priorityAnalysis.intro: Both documents independently converge on ~12 recurring domains, ranked by how often each actually appears across real past recall papers rather than by curriculum weighting — a different, complementary lens to the official syllabus breakdown above.

goldenRules.text: Never skip stats. There are 40–50 stats questions per paper — getting most of them right is the difference between passing and failing.
The same LD syndrome questions come up every session. Learn one good table covering all 12 syndromes and you will get most of these marks.
Prevention questions are the easiest marks in the exam — the same 5 scenarios recycle every session. Memorise the definitions once and bank these 3–4 marks every time.
For psychotherapy: the distinction between CAT (3 Rs, goodbye letters), DBT (phone calls, hierarchy), and the family-therapy model types is tested in every paper.
For ECT: retrograde (explicit) memory is most affected; bilateral > unilateral efficacy but more cognitive side effects; QTc >500ms = emergency dose reduction.

1st priority: statistics every single day — calculations, test selection, graph reading (30–35% of the paper). 2nd: LD syndromes + drugs in pregnancy + ECT facts (low effort, guaranteed marks). 3rd: psychotherapy terms + prevention scenarios (1–2 hours total). 4th: pharmacology special-situation drug choices + dementia differentials. 5th: forensic statistics + child-psychiatry NICE guidelines.

repeatedFacts.text: Diagnostic-test statistics (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, LR+, LR−, post-test odds) appear EVERY session, multiple questions each time.
Exam favourite worked example: pre-test probability 1/8, Sn 80%, Sp 80% → pre-test odds 1/7 × LR+ 4 = post-test odds 4/7 — appeared in Sep 2022, Mar 2023, and Mock 14.
ANCOVA vs ANOVA (adjusting for a covariate such as age) is a frequently tested trap — appeared in Oct 2023, Jun 2023, and May 2025.
Case-control → odds ratio; cohort → relative risk. Risk ratio CANNOT be calculated from a case-control study (no population denominator).
Block randomisation (ensures equal numbers per arm) is the most frequently tested randomisation question.
Audit-loop trap: a re-audit done with no changes implemented in between means the audit loop is incomplete — appeared in Sep 2022, Oct 2023, and the compiled Recalls Solved file.
STARD (diagnostic accuracy reporting) specifically appeared in Mar 2023 and May 2025.
Forest-plot, Kaplan-Meier, and CONSORT-diagram EMI stems use new numbers every session but test the same interpretation skills — practise reading them, don't memorise specific figures.
Full statistical-test decision table and formula sheet.

expectedNote.text: There are 40–50 stats questions per paper; getting most of them right is described as the difference between passing and failing, regardless of clinical knowledge — the single highest-expected-value topic to keep drilling right up to the exam.

domains.title: Clinical Pharmacology (pregnancy, EPSEs, mood stabilisers, clozapine)

repeatedFacts.text: Drugs-in-pregnancy / neonatal-effects EMI appears in EVERY paper.
Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in both pregnancy and breastfeeding (least placental/milk exposure); lithium is contraindicated in breastfeeding.
Tardive dyskinesia management trap: the first step is to STOP the anticholinergic (e.g. procyclidine) — anticholinergics worsen TD — before reducing/switching the antipsychotic.
Lithium RAISES calcium, opposite to carbamazepine, valproate and haloperidol, which lower it.
If clozapine isn't working, the first step is to check compliance (clozapine level) before anything else; amisulpride augmentation has the best evidence for partial response.
QTc >500ms → reduce dose immediately and consider urgent cardiology referral; risperidone+citalopram and citalopram+diphenhydramine are named high-risk combinations.
Neonatal-presentation EMI (classic, tested every session): opioids → jittery/high-pitched cry; cocaine → overarousal/tachycardia; sodium valproate → cleft palate + developmental delay.

expectedNote.text: Drug-choice-in-special-situations tables (post-MI, epilepsy, renal/liver impairment, tamoxifen, breastfeeding) recur across sessions in near-identical form — learning the table once covers most of this domain's marks.

domains.title: Intellectual Disability & Genetics
domains.effortReward: Low effort once the table is learnt

repeatedFacts.text: The same LD syndromes are tested repeatedly across every recall session — the full 12-syndrome comparison table (genetics, clinical features, exam clue) is worth memorising in one sitting.
Genomic imprinting is a specifically recurring point: Prader-Willi = paternal deletion 15q; Angelman = maternal deletion 15q — tested in Mar 2024 and the compiled Recalls Solved file.
Most common cause of intellectual disability overall = unknown (up to 60%); chromosomal = Down syndrome; inherited/genetic = Fragile X; environmental/acquired = foetal alcohol syndrome.
5–7 questions on the same syndrome set appear every session.

expectedNote.text: "Learn ONE good table covering all 12 syndromes and you will get most of these marks" — the source's own framing after cross-referencing 8 recall sources.

domains.title: Dementia & Old Age Psychiatry (DLB, Alzheimer's, FTD, MCI)

repeatedFacts.text: "Which dementia is irreversible?" is frequently tested — answer MND/ALS; reversible causes (NPH, chronic subdural haematoma, Wilson's disease, pellagra, alcohol) are the distractor set.
DLB's core feature — REM sleep behaviour disorder, which can precede cognitive decline by years — and its supportive feature, severe neuroleptic sensitivity, are repeatedly tested.
Best tool to differentiate MCI from dementia is informant assessment of activities of daily living, NOT MMSE or MoCA scores alone.
Risperidone is the only UK-licensed antipsychotic for BPSD in moderate-severe Alzheimer's.
MCI converts to Alzheimer's at roughly 9.6% (range 5–15%) per year.

CAT's 3 Rs (Reformulation → Recognition → Revision) plus its goodbye letters, DBT's phone-calls-as-core-technique plus its behaviour hierarchy, and the four family-therapy model distinctions are tested in every paper.
Most-tested family-therapy distinction: Systemic/Milan = re-framing + hypothesising; Strategic = paradoxical injunctions; Structural = unspoken rules + hierarchy; Narrative = externalisation.
DBT trap: it is NOT based on psychodynamic formulations and is NOT delivered only in groups — both are common wrong-option distractors.
Motivational Interviewing (DEARS) and IPT (RIIG) mnemonics recur as EMI option sets.
Prison suicide risk is 3–8× higher in males and >10× higher in females than the general population; remand status carries HIGHER risk than sentenced status (the reverse of intuition).
Pritchard fitness-to-plead criteria: amnesia for the offence does NOT make someone unfit to plead; learning disability is the most common cause of unfitness.

Sane automatism = external cause (concussion, one-off hypoglycaemia, sleep terrors) → complete acquittal. Insane automatism = internal cause (epilepsy, sleepwalking, brain tumour) → not guilty by reason of insanity.
Key legal cases recur as a set: Bournewood (DoLS), Tarasoff (duty to warn), Osman v UK (police duty to warn), Gillick/Fraser (minors' consent), Bolam (negligence standard).
ASPD prevalence in the male prison population is consistently cited at ~50%.

expectedNote.text: Forensic questions test specific memorised numbers rather than concepts — the source frames this as "once learnt, reliable marks; learn the numbers, not just the concepts."

repeatedFacts.text: ADHD heritability (70–80%) is the highest of all listed childhood psychiatric conditions.
Paediatric OCD drug-licensing ages are a specific recurring trap: sertraline from age 6, fluvoxamine from age 8; clomipramine is NOT first-line and needs cardiac monitoring.
Mild depression watchful-waiting period is 2 WEEKS, not 6 weeks or 2 months — a commonly-tested exact-number trap; fluoxetine's minimum licensed age is 5 years.
Tourette syndrome requires 2+ motor tics AND 1+ vocal tic for over a year; M:F ratio 2–5:1.
Refeeding syndrome's most dangerous electrolyte disturbance is hypophosphataemia (not hypokalaemia, though that also occurs).
MEED admission red flags recur as an exact-number set: HR <40, BMI <13 (adult), temperature <35.5°C, QTc >430ms (male)/>450ms (female), K+ <2.5.
Postpartum blues affects up to 50% of new mothers; postpartum depression 10–15%; postpartum psychosis 1–2 per 1000 deliveries; BPAD postpartum relapse risk ~50%.
The same ~5 prevention scenarios recycle every single session — described as the easiest marks in the whole exam.
At-risk mental state for psychosis + CBT is BOTH primary prevention AND indicated prevention — always select two answers when this scenario appears.
Universal prevention for alcohol in the community = increasing the price per unit, the most evidence-backed answer; school-based education is also universal.
Full scenario-to-classification table (school anti-bullying, low-income family support, lithium prophylaxis, alcohol pricing, screening).

expectedNote.text: "1 hour of learning = 3–4 guaranteed marks" — the source's own estimate of return on effort for this domain.

repeatedFacts.text: Retrograde (explicit/episodic) memory is the most affected memory type; the only absolute contraindication is phaeochromocytoma.
Bilateral placement is more effective than unilateral but causes more cognitive side effects.
Psychotic depression is the best predictor of ECT response — not severity of depression.
ECT combined with lithium carries a ×12 risk of delirium.
Alcohol and benzodiazepines are the ONLY substances with life-threatening withdrawal; opioid withdrawal is very unpleasant but not life-threatening.
Chlordiazepoxide is standard first-line for alcohol detox; oxazepam is preferred in liver disease/COPD; disulfiram is a deterrent, not relapse prevention (that's naltrexone/acamprosate).
Alcohol is the only substance that is both a GABA-A agonist AND an NMDA antagonist.

domains.title: Old Age Psychiatry & Other Clinical Topics

repeatedFacts.text: This is the source's own catch-all lower-priority bucket for older-adult clinical content not already folded into the Dementia domain above — ranked 12th of 12 domains by revision priority.

independentAnalysis.methodology: Built directly from this app's own corpus rather than citing the two documents above: (1) a mechanical keyword-frequency count across all 1578 already-parsed, already-cited mock-exam questions (content/questions/mock-*.json, 14 exams); (2) five real recall/answer-key PDFs from resources/paper-b/previous-year-question-source/ (Sep 2022, Mar 2023, Jun 2023, Oct 2023, and a compiled "Recalls solved"), read page-by-page with every extracted fact spot-checked against the source PDF. Two further free-form recall files in the same folder (Mar 2024, May 2025) have no page markers and a lot of hedged, uncertain phrasing, so — consistent with this app's existing stance on that folder — they were read for corroboration only, never cited as an individual fact. A web search for current trend commentary found nothing beyond the same handful of sites already reflected in the Priority & Recall Analysis branch; the two url-cited points below are the only web additions.

repeatedTopics.text: Schizophrenia is the single most recurring clinical topic in this app's mock corpus — 152 questions across 14/14 of this app's own mock exams.
Diagnostic-test-statistics questions (sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV) recur most consistently of any stats subtopic — 45 questions across 14/14 of this app's own mock exams.
Lithium-related questions (toxicity, monitoring, teratogenicity) recur across almost every mock — 71 questions across 13/14 of this app's own mock exams.
Alzheimer's disease recurs across every single mock exam analysed — 58 questions across 14/14 of this app's own mock exams.
Clozapine (augmentation, monitoring, contraindications) recurs across every mock exam analysed — 52 questions across 14/14 of this app's own mock exams.
Suicide risk within 1 year of self-harm (~0.7%; 1.1% males, 0.5% females) is quoted with the exact same figures in two independently-written recall sessions (Sep 2022 and Oct 2023).
Retrograde memory as the type most affected by ECT is tested in both the Oct 2023 and Mar 2023 recall sessions, each with near-identical explanation wording.
Sane automatism (external cause → acquittal) vs insane automatism (internal/recurring cause → not guilty by reason of insanity) is tested in the Jun 2023, Mar 2023, and Sep 2022 sessions alike.
Cri-du-chat's features (high-pitched cat-like cry, hypertelorism, micrognathia, epicanthic folds) are recited in near-identical wording across the Mar 2023, Sep 2022, and Jun 2023 recalls.
DiGeorge/22q11.2's CATCH-22 mnemonic (Cardiac, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcaemia) is named identically in both Mar 2023 and Jun 2023.
Rett syndrome's MECP2 gene, X-linked, girls-only presentation with regression at 6–18 months recurs across the Jun 2023 and Sep 2022 recalls.
Pritchard fitness-to-plead criteria recur in both the Mar 2023 and Sep 2022 recalls, each listing the same six components.
Bournewood (DoLS) and Tarasoff (duty to warn) are named as a case pair in the Mar 2023 recall's legal-cases section, matching the same pairing this app's own study guides already flag.
Prader-Willi's equal (1:1) male:female prevalence is highlighted independently in both the Jun 2023 recall and the Recalls Solved compilation.
QTc >500ms → reduce dose immediately and consider cardiology referral is stated in near-identical wording in both the Sep 2022 and Jun 2023 recalls.
Block randomisation (equal group sizes, larger blocks = less predictable) is explained in matching terms in the Oct 2023 and Sep 2022 recalls.
PRISMA having replaced QUOROM as the systematic-review reporting standard is stated in both the Mar 2023 and Sep 2022 recalls.
Refeeding syndrome's mechanism (carbohydrate-driven insulin release causing intracellular phosphate/potassium/magnesium shift) is explained almost identically in the Oct 2023 and Sep 2022 recalls.

concentrationTopics.text: Statistics: diagnostic-test calculations are this app's single highest-yield subtopic by mock-exam volume — 45 questions across 14/14 of this app's own mock exams.
Learning Disability: the 12-syndrome comparison table (genetics, features, exam clue) is the densest single recurring block across all 5 analysed recall sessions — memorise it once.
Adult Psychiatry: schizophrenia and mood-disorder management dominate this app's mock-exam question volume — 152 questions across 14/14 of this app's own mock exams.
Old Age Psychiatry: dementia differentials (Alzheimer's, DLB, vascular, FTD) are the most tested old-age subtopic — 58 questions across 14/14 of this app's own mock exams.

Forensic Psychiatry: named legal cases (Bournewood, Tarasoff, Osman, Gillick, Pritchard) plus specific memorised numbers (prison suicide rates, recidivism %) appear across 4 of the 5 analysed recall sessions.
Perinatal Psychiatry: the drugs-in-pregnancy/neonatal-effects EMI format appears in 4 of the 5 analysed recall sessions.
Psychotherapy: CAT/DBT/family-therapy terminology is tested in 4 of the 5 analysed recall sessions, always as short factual-recall items rather than scenario reasoning.
Addiction Psychiatry: alcohol-withdrawal timeline and drug-specific withdrawal features appear in 3 of the 5 analysed recall sessions.
Child & Adolescent Psychiatry: ADHD/OCD/depression NICE-guideline drug-choice questions appear in 3 of the 5 analysed recall sessions.
Evidence-Based Medicine: reporting-guideline matching (CONSORT/PRISMA/STROBE/STARD/MOOSE) appears in 3 of the 5 analysed recall sessions.
Research Methods: intention-to-treat vs per-protocol analysis, and randomisation/stratification distinctions, appear in 4 of the 5 analysed recall sessions.
Epidemiology: Susser's criteria for causation (association, time order, direction as the three essential elements) appear in 3 of the 5 analysed recall sessions.

expectedTopics.text: Diagnostic-test-statistics worked calculations (Sn/Sp/LR+/post-test odds) have been the single most consistent question type across both this app's own mocks (all 14) and 4 of 5 analysed recall sessions — expect several worked-calculation stems again, with new numbers testing the same method.

The LD syndrome comparison table's content has stayed essentially unchanged since at least the Sep 2022 session — a future paper is far more likely to re-test an existing syndrome than introduce a new one.
Fitness to plead, automatism, and diminished responsibility recur as a paired forensic-legal trio across multiple sessions — expect at least one of the three each sitting.

QTc-prolongation combination stems (a specific drug pairing plus an electrolyte or comorbidity) have appeared in most analysed sessions in slightly different combinations — expect the same stem shape with different drugs.

The BALANCE (lithium vs valproate) and CUtLASS (FGA vs SGA efficacy) named trials recur as a pair in mood-stabiliser/antipsychotic-choice questions across sessions — worth knowing both by name and headline finding.
Reporting-guideline matching (which acronym goes with which study type) has appeared in three of the five analysed sessions with the same 6-8 guidelines each time — a fixed, learnable set.
Genomic imprinting (Prader-Willi = paternal deletion, Angelman = maternal deletion, Fragile X = imprinting error) has recurred every session analysed and is a strong candidate to recur again.

Independent exam-prep commentary describes MRCPsych Paper B statistics as "highly predictable and concept-driven" once the recurring calculation types are learned, and notes that tables/flowcharts repeat with new numbers each session rather than new concepts — consistent with what this app's own corpus analysis found.

Paper B is commonly described online as splitting revision effort roughly evenly between clinical psychiatry and statistics/critical appraisal, even though critical review alone carries 33.5% of marks — worth weighting revision time accordingly rather than by mark share alone.

points.text: Early-onset schizophrenia (vs adult-onset) shows poorer premorbid functioning, earlier developmental delays, and more impaired global IQ.
Worse first-episode-psychosis outcome predictors: longer duration of untreated psychosis, male gender, non-adherence, poor premorbid adjustment, insidious onset, and comorbid substance use.
DSM-5 requires 5 of 9 criteria for borderline personality disorder, including unstable self-image/relationships, impulsivity, self-harm, affective instability, micro-psychosis, and chronic emptiness.
First-episode psychosis is treated with low-to-moderate dose antipsychotic monotherapy — well below doses used in established illness.
Bipolar diagnosis is commonly delayed 8–10 years, is misdiagnosed in 20–60% of cases, and bipolar I is more diagnostically stable over time than bipolar II.
In Alzheimer's BPSD, apathy is the most frequent symptom, ahead of depression, aggression, anxiety, and sleep disturbance.

In renal impairment, haloperidol (low dose) is generally preferred; sulpiride/amisulpride should be avoided as they're renally cleared, and clozapine/chlorpromazine avoided for urinary retention risk.
Extrapyramidal side-effect prevalence with older antipsychotics: dystonia ~10%, pseudo-parkinsonism ~20–25%, akathisia ~20–25%, tardive dyskinesia ~5% per year of exposure.
Around delivery, lithium is suspended 24–48h before a planned induction/C-section, checked 12h after the last dose, and restarted on postnatal day 1.
Lithium monitoring in pregnancy is typically every 4 weeks until 34 weeks, then weekly until 2 weeks postpartum.
Valproate exposure in pregnancy causes major malformations in up to 11% of children, including cleft palate, neural tube defects (1–2%), and developmental delay/autism.
Paroxetine at high first-trimester dose is linked to cardiac malformations (VSD/ASD) — the highest cardiac risk of the SSRIs.
Quetiapine is considered relatively safe in pregnancy due to low placental transfer; NICE favours it as an alternative to a mood stabiliser during pregnancy.
For breastfeeding, lithium is contraindicated (40–50% of maternal serum level passes into milk); paroxetine has a lower milk/plasma ratio than fluoxetine or sertraline.
Late-pregnancy SSRI exposure carries a small absolute increased risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, particularly with short-half-life drugs like paroxetine and venlafaxine.
Ictal eye closure favours psychogenic non-epileptic seizures over true epileptic seizures; PNES episodes also tend to last longer (>2 minutes suggestive, >10 minutes strongly suggestive).
Poor outcome after traumatic brain injury is linked to longer loss of consciousness, longer post-traumatic amnesia (>24h), older age, and reduced pre-injury cognitive reserve.
rTMS is contraindicated with ferromagnetic/magnetic-sensitive implants near the coil field, and cautioned in prior stroke, brain tumour, or epilepsy.

ICD-11's dissociative neurological symptom disorder (with speech disturbance) covers dysphonia/aphonia/dysarthria of psychological cause, often preceded by conflict or stress, not produced intentionally.

NMS risk factors include high ambient temperature, dehydration, agitation/catatonia, rapid antipsychotic dose escalation, withdrawal of anti-parkinsonian medication, and depot/high-potency antipsychotics.
Malignant catatonia can mimic NMS with immobility, rigidity, mutism, posturing, and excessive motor activity, and shares pathophysiological features with it.
Lorazepam is first-line for catatonic/affective stupor, with rapid onset of benefit when effective (doses of 4mg/day up to 8–24mg/day if needed).
QTc-prolongation risk factors: female sex, extremes of age, bradycardia/heart failure, liver disease, hypokalaemia/hypocalcaemia/hypomagnesaemia, stimulant use, and starvation.
Delirium tremens starts 3–4 days after the last drink, occurs in 3–5% of those withdrawing, and carries 10–20% mortality if untreated.
Lithium toxicity (>1.2mmol/L) presents with polyuria, abdominal pain, fine tremor, and myoclonic twitches.
Rivastigmine has the best evidence in DLB/Parkinson's disease dementia — a large RCT (McKeith et al 2006) showed it alleviated hallucinations, delusions, anxiety, and apathy.
The greatest risk factors for vascular dementia are high systolic and diastolic blood pressure, acting via stroke risk and white-matter change.
MoCA (2005) is a 30-item, ~10-minute update to the MMSE (1975), available in 35+ languages, but cannot itself differentiate dementia subtypes.
Alzheimer's risk is ~1% at 60, ~5% at 65, doubling roughly every 5 years, reaching ~40% by age 85.
First-degree relatives of an Alzheimer's proband carry a 15–19% risk (vs 5% controls); APOE4 homozygotes carry 10–30× the risk of non-carriers.
Frontotemporal dementia is highly heritable (~30% strong family history), mostly via autosomal dominant C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT mutations.

DLB's core features (mnemonic REM-PCV) are fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder, and spontaneous parkinsonism, with neuroleptic sensitivity as a supportive feature.

A third of late-life dementia risk is attributed to seven modifiable factors (low education, midlife hypertension/obesity, diabetes, inactivity, smoking, depression) — smoking has the largest population attributable fraction.
CAT's sequential diagrammatic reformulation (a visual flow-chart of the target problem procedure) is its distinguishing technique, built on the 3 Rs.
'Acting out' is illustrated by missed therapy appointments or increased substance use precisely when therapeutic work becomes difficult.
Displacement redirects emotion toward a safer target — separating the feeling from its real object to avoid confronting what's actually threatening.
Yalom's therapeutic factors include catharsis, altruism, group cohesion, interpersonal learning, and installation of hope.
Behavioural activation uses the TRAP model (Trigger, Response, Avoidance Pattern) to assess avoidance, aiming to replace it with TRAC (Alternate Coping).
Motivational Interviewing's DEARS (Developing discrepancy, Empathy, Avoid arguments, Rolling with resistance, Support self-efficacy) starts by amplifying cognitive dissonance.
DBT (Linehan, 1991) takes a hierarchical view of goals: reducing self-harm first, then therapy-interfering behaviours, then quality-of-life-diminishing behaviours.
Atomoxetine is used when tics emerge as a side effect of stimulant treatment; clonidine/guanfacine is used when a comorbid tic disorder isn't secondary to stimulant use.
ICD-11 requires ADHD symptoms be evident before age 12.
Sertraline (from age 6) and fluvoxamine (from age 8) are the SSRIs licensed for paediatric OCD in the UK; paroxetine isn't recommended in this age group.

Fluoxetine is the only antidepressant licensed for depression under 18 in the UK, creating a treatment dilemma when depression and OCD co-occur (since only fluvoxamine/sertraline are licensed for paediatric OCD).
PTSD identification in children improves by asking the child directly about their experiences rather than relying only on caregiver history; drug treatment isn't routinely recommended.
ADHD heritability (70–80%) is the highest of the listed childhood psychiatric conditions, with a 2–3× increased risk in siblings.
Landau-Kleffner syndrome is a childhood epilepsy syndrome with onset usually before age 6, twice as common in boys.
Amphetamine/cocaine withdrawal features hypersomnia, hyperphagia, depression ('crash'), irritability, agitation, and vivid dreams.
Withdrawal psychosis occurs with alcohol and benzodiazepines but not typically with cannabis, cocaine, or heroin withdrawal.
LSD carries no overdose risk and causes no physiological dependence or withdrawal — the least dependence-forming of the common illicit drugs.
Amphetamine-induced psychosis resembles schizophrenia but with prominent visual/tactile hallucinations, hyperactivity, disinhibited behaviour, and little formal thought disorder.
Around 30% of dependent cocaine users (and 12% of recreational users) show clinically relevant cognitive impairment, especially in sustained attention and working memory.
Mephedrone is a synthetic cathinone stimulant (cathinone itself from the khat plant), producing effects similar to cocaine, MDMA, and amphetamines.
Chronic ketamine use causes urinary tract symptoms (frequency, urgency, haematuria) via interstitial cystitis in up to 30% of users.
Arson is most commonly associated with substance use disorders (especially alcohol) and antisocial personality disorder, alongside psychotic disorders and low intellectual functioning.
Victims of female homicide perpetrators are often under 16; 13% of filicide perpetrators go on to suicide.
Female intimate-partner-homicide perpetrators are most commonly aged 30–39 (average age 35).

Among homicide perpetrators, 30% have a recorded mental disorder — personality disorder is the single most common diagnosis (27%), ahead of schizophrenia, substance use, and affective disorder (18% each of that 30%).
Of indecent exposure offenders, 20% are first-time offenders and 20–30% reoffend; most have a prior history of sexual or non-sexual offending.
Half of mentally ill perpetrators of child homicide have a psychotic disorder, and victims are disproportionately under 16.
Mens rea (guilty mind/intent) and actus reus (the guilty act) are both required for an offence; mens rea cannot exist if a mental abnormality removes capacity for rational intent.
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (X-linked recessive, HPRT gene) causes hyperuricaemia, spasticity, choreiform movements, and severe self-mutilating biting behaviour.

Down syndrome is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability, Fragile X the most common inherited cause, and foetal alcohol syndrome the most common acquired cause; up to 60% of cases have no identifiable cause.
Functional behavioural analysis (assessing behaviour, situation, consequence, and reinforcer) is the gold-standard first step before managing aggression or self-injury in intellectual disability.
The normalisation principle argues people with intellectual disability should experience normal patterns of everyday life — changing the environment, not the individual.
Diagnostic overshadowing describes clinicians attributing new physical or mental symptoms to a patient's pre-existing learning disability rather than investigating them.
IQ bands: mild 50–69 (~85% of ID), moderate 35–49 (~10%), severe 20–34 (~3–4%), profound <20 (~1–2%, developmental level of a one-year-old).
Recall distinguishes Lesch-Nyhan (severe self-mutilation) from Prader-Willi, Cri du Chat, Cornelia de Lange, and Smith-Magenis as EMI options for the same self-harm scenario.

Nolan's Model for Improvement structures quality-improvement work around three questions: what are we trying to accomplish, how will we know a change is an improvement, and what changes will produce that improvement.
Direct costs (staff, drugs, hospital space) are distinguished from indirect costs (lost patient/carer productivity) and intangible costs (pain, suffering, stigma) when costing a service.
Sex-ratio table: Tourette's 2–5:1, ADHD (children) 2:1, ASD 4–5:1, Asperger's 5:1, depression 1:2, anorexia 1:9, bulimia 1:9, BPD 1:3 (male:female unless noted).
Schizophrenia risk is 9% in siblings and 13% in children of an affected person (vs 1% general population); 17% in dizygotic twins and 48% in monozygotic twins.
Almost all adults with Down syndrome develop Alzheimer's-like neuropathology by age 40, with amyloid pathology preceding cognitive impairment by 15–20 years.
Mean imputation of missing data in an ITT analysis injects false precision and increases the risk of a Type 1 (false positive) error.
Randomisation controls both known and unknown confounders at the design stage; stratification controls confounders (and effect modifiers) at the analysis stage.
Non-parametric test pairings: Wilcoxon signed-rank ↔ paired t-test, Mann-Whitney U ↔ unpaired t-test, Kruskal-Wallis ↔ one-way ANOVA.
Cox proportional hazards assumes the hazard ratio between groups is constant over time; the log-rank test, unlike Cox regression, cannot adjust for other explanatory variables.
Risk ratio can't be calculated in a case-control study (no true population denominator) — only odds ratio can; cohort studies allow direct relative-risk calculation.
Per-protocol analysis (compliant patients only) is the antithesis of intention-to-treat and is better suited to testing a drug's biological efficacy than its real-world effectiveness.
Imputing missing/unpublished smaller studies on a funnel plot reduces the risk of a Type 2 error and makes the plot more representative of true effect.
Both the Galbraith plot and the forest plot can be used to check for heterogeneity between studies.

The Belmont Report (1976, US National Commission) and the Declaration of Helsinki (1964, updated 2000/2002/2004) both set ethical principles for human-subject research, distinct from the Nuremberg Code's post-WWII focus on experimentation.
Fisher's exact test is required instead of chi-square when any expected cell value in a comparison table falls below 5.

A fixed-effects meta-analysis model assumes one shared true effect across studies and should only be used once heterogeneity is safely excluded; a random-effects model is used when heterogeneity exists and gives proportionally more weight to smaller studies.
The F-statistic is the ratio of two variances.
A very small p-value (e.g. 0.01) paired with a very narrow confidence interval typically signals a large sample size.
NNT = 1/ARR, where ARR (absolute risk reduction) = EER − CER (experimental minus control event rate).
Worked SEM example: SD 16, n 12 → SEM = 16/√12 ≈ 4.62.
If a test's sensitivity increases at a fixed cut-off, the false-positive rate rises and specificity falls, because a lower threshold catches more true positives but also more false positives.
Worked example: pre-test probability 1/8, sensitivity 80%, specificity 80% → pre-test odds 1/7, LR+ = 0.8/0.2 = 4, post-test odds = 1/7 × 4 = 4/7.

Formal definitions: sensitivity = proportion of diseased correctly identified; specificity = proportion of well correctly excluded; PPV = proportion of positive results truly diseased; NPV = proportion of negative results truly disease-free.

sections.title: Organisation and Delivery of Psychiatric Services

recurringTraps.text: Tertiary prevention means reducing handicap/disability from established disease (i.e. rehabilitation), **NOT** eliminating the illness itself — a frequently mis-selected option is 'reducing incidence', which describes primary, not tertiary, prevention.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Psychiatric Services_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Universal vs selective prevention in pregnancy-related interventions is a fine distinction: improving prenatal nutrition/antenatal care broadly (all pregnant women) is classed as **UNIVERSAL** prevention, whereas targeting a specific risk factor like low birth weight within pregnant women is classed as **SELECTIVE** prevention (see the linked **EMI**) — the exam expects you to track whether the whole population or only a risk-defined subgroup is targeted.

recurringTraps.text: Rose's Prevention Paradox is regularly tested with near-identical distractor wording ('universal is best for individuals' vs 'high-risk targeting is best for individuals but universal wins at population level') — read to the end of each option before choosing; the two SBAs sampled here use almost the same stem with subtly reordered clauses.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Psychiatric Services_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Early recognition of alcohol misuse using screening questionnaires is **SECONDARY** prevention (early detection of existing/incipient cases), not primary — a frequently mis-selected option in 'which is **NOT** primary prevention' framing.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Psychiatric Services_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: In the schizophrenia-prevention **EMI**, targeting pregnant women to address low birth weight is **SELECTIVE** prevention (a defined risk factor within a subgroup), while targeting the general urban social milieu is **UNIVERSAL** prevention, and identifying a preschizophrenic/prodromal state is **INDICATED** prevention — three different classifications for three superficially similar 'early action in psychosis' scenarios.

recurringTraps.text: Pregnancy is a **RELATIVE** contraindication to **ECT**, not absolute — the book notes state there are no absolute contraindications to **ECT** at all, which itself is a frequently tested standalone fact.

recurringTraps.text: "Which comorbidity should be treated first?" → **NICE** explicitly wants comorbid depression treated **BEFORE** anxiety — treating anxiety first is presented as the wrong (non-recommended) answer.

recurringTraps.text: "Do antidepressants increase suicide risk?" — the expected, guideline-backed answer is that suicides occur **MORE** often among those **NOT** on an antidepressant; don't let the black-box-warning framing pull you toward the intuitive-but-wrong answer.

recurringTraps.text: **Lithium** toxicity with neurological symptoms → haemodialysis is the expected answer once levels exceed the life-threatening 2.0 mmol/L threshold, not simply stopping the drug.

recurringTraps.text: Risk of schizophrenia if **BOTH** parents affected is 40–==50%== — don't confuse with the single first-degree-relative figure of 12–==15%==; both numbers are tested.

recurringTraps.text: Cannabis by age 15 confers a fourfold (not the general twofold) increased schizophrenia risk — the exam distinguishes the age-15 figure from the overall-adolescent figure.

recurringTraps.text: Even when a bipolar-disorder stem emphasises medication-free status while trying to conceive and evokes postpartum psychosis/mania, the statistically most likely tested outcome is relapse into depression after delivery — mania/psychosis are more dramatic, but depression is the most prevalent postpartum relapse type overall.

recurringTraps.text: The 'most sensitive period for foetal malformation' is tested in the question bank as weeks 2–14 (citing **NICE** 2020) — a wider window than the **SPMM** book's 'weeks 6–10 most vulnerable' framing. Go with whichever framing the stem's cited guideline points to.

recurringTraps.text: Neural tube defects are **NOT** an **SSRI** risk in pregnancy — that is a **valproate** association. The tested **SSRI** risks are neonatal irritability, spontaneous abortion, prematurity and reduced birth weight.

recurringTraps.text: Three different antidepressant/relapse statistics are tested for this topic and are easy to conflate: a 5-fold relative risk of relapse on stopping antidepressants generally, a ==70%== relapse rate specifically in psychiatric-setting cohorts with recurrent depression who discontinue medication, and a ==40%== relapse rate in pregnancies of women with recurrent major depression more generally — check exactly what population/exposure the stem specifies before picking a number.

recurringTraps.text: Post-**MI** depression: **sertraline** (**SADHART**) is the drug of choice - **fluvoxamine** and **citalopram**/**escitalopram** should specifically be avoided, and antidepressants are generally avoided in the first 2 months post-**MI** regardless of drug choice.

recurringTraps.text: 'Except' (false statement) question: the most common **METHOD** of suicide does **NOT** remain the same across countries (it varies with lethality/availability of means, e.g. pesticides vs analgesics) — this is the false statement to identify among otherwise-true epidemiological facts.

recurringTraps.text: Among several plausible-sounding options, the **TRUE** statement about suicide epidemiology is that suicide statistics have low reliability (due to variable coroner recording and cultural reporting bias) — the exam surrounds this with several confidently-worded **FALSE** statements (recessions decrease suicide, comparable rates across nations, wars increase suicide, declining rates in young men) to test whether you can spot the one accurate claim.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Emergency Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: As high as ==90%== of people who die by suicide in high-income countries were experiencing a mental illness at the time — a frequently tested headline figure distinct from the lower per-disorder psychological-autopsy percentages.

recurringTraps.text: The classically-quoted ~==10%== lifetime suicide risk in schizophrenia is outdated; the exam expects the corrected meta-analytic figure of ~==6%== (==5.6%==, Palmer 2005) from studies with adequate follow-up — don't default to the older, higher number.

recurringTraps.text: 'Except' question: dementia is the diagnosis **WITHOUT** a clearly-raised completed-suicide rate (unlike alcohol dependence, depression, mania, schizophrenia) — the literature on dementia and suicide is genuinely mixed, and the exam expects you to know that nuance rather than assume all cognitive/psychiatric illness raises risk equally.

recurringTraps.text: **EEG** periodic sharp-wave complexes are a sporadic-**CJD** feature that the exam explicitly excludes from variant **CJD** — a "which prion disease shows this **EEG** pattern" **EMI** item expects you to know the absence in vCJD, not just the presence in sporadic disease.

recurringTraps.text: **NINCDS-ADRDA** probable-**AD** criteria trap: cerebral atrophy on **CT** is **NOT** a required criterion (it only helps exclude other causes) — a frequently tested "which is **NOT** required" question.

recurringTraps.text: **CAMDEX** vs **CAMDEX-R** vs **CAMCOG** is a recurring confusable set: **CAMDEX** is the full instrument (structured interview + informant interview + physical exam + **CAMCOG** cognitive battery), **CAMCOG** is specifically its cognitive subscale, and **DMR** (not **CAMDEX**/**MMSE**) is the correct screening tool for dementia in people with intellectual disability.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Old Age Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: "Which feature correlates with **AD** severity?" — clinically evident depression is the odd one out: depression becomes **LESS** common as **AD** progresses from moderate to severe, unlike most other features that track severity.

recurringTraps.text: The Duff (2004) **CSM** restriction (**olanzapine**/**risperidone** associated with a 2x stroke risk increase in dementia) is deliberately contrasted with Herrmann et al (2004), who found **NO** significant difference in stroke risk vs typical neuroleptics — both study findings are independently examinable, and the exam expects you to know the regulatory position (Duff/**CSM**) governs practice regardless of the conflicting evidence (Herrmann).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Old Age Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: 'Interpretation of the transference is the **ONLY** means to access the unconscious' is the **INCORRECT** statement to spot — dreams, free association, slips of the tongue and abreaction are all valid routes too. recurringTraps.text: Defence mechanisms are a function of the **EGO** specifically (Anna Freud, 1936) — not the Id, Superego, or a combination; a single-structure answer is required despite the temptation to hedge with 'both'.

recurringTraps.text: A vignette where nursing staff feel 'unwanted' and angry toward a personality-disordered patient is keyed to Counter-transference as the best single answer, even though the explanation's actual mechanism described is projective identification (the patient's projected hatred is taken in and acted out by staff) — the exam wants the broader phenomenon name, not the specific Kleinian mechanism.

recurringTraps.text: 'A diagnosis of paraphrenia' is the answer to spot among positive prognostic indicators for psychotherapy — psychotic disorders are traditionally viewed as involving ego disintegration and are **NOT** a positive predictor, unlike self-scrutiny, response to trial interpretation, some medication response, and psychological mindedness.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Psychotherapy Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Poor response to psychodynamic psychotherapy is predicted by a history of multiple 'acting out' incidents — **NOT** by lower socioeconomic status or average **IQ**, which the explanation explicitly states are not, by themselves, poor predictors (counters an intuitive but wrong assumption).

recurringTraps.text: The Premack Principle ('Grandma's rule' — high-frequency behaviour reinforces a low-frequency one, e.g. finishing homework before play) is a specifically named operant concept distinct from plain positive reinforcement — worth knowing by name for **EMI** matching.

recurringTraps.text: Pemoline is no longer licensed in the **UK** for **ADHD** (hepatotoxicity/liver failure risk) — a specific 'which drug is delisted' recall question, not a first-line-choice question.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/EMIs Child Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: **ICD-11**'s 'harmful pattern of use' (damage already caused) is time-defined (>=12 months episodic **OR** >=1 month continuous use), whereas 'hazardous substance use' (increased risk, no harm yet) has explicitly **NO** defined time period - the exam tests this asymmetry directly.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: "Which feature is **NOT** in the Edwards & Gross (1976) criteria?" -> the distractor 'decreased tolerance' is wrong on two counts: tolerance in dependence is **INCREASED**, and impaired control (not tolerance direction) is the concept that was never in the original 1976 list at all (it was added later by **ICD**/**DSM**).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Lactate dehydrogenase is a distractor, **NOT** a recognised marker of excess alcohol use - the real markers are raised **MCV**, raised **GGT** and carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (**CDT**), plus anaemia/thrombocytopenia/neutropenia/raised LFTs.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Counter-intuitive pharmacokinetics: gastrectomy **INCREASES** alcohol absorption/intoxication risk (less time for gastric alcohol dehydrogenase to break it down), while conditions that **SLOW** gastric emptying (e.g. pyloric stenosis) can **REDUCE** acute intoxication - the opposite of what test-takers often assume about surgery and alcohol tolerance.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Opioid withdrawal pupils are **DILATED**, not constricted - pupillary constriction is a feature of opioid **INTOXICATION**/overdose. This exact reversal is tested repeatedly across the question bank as 'which is **NOT**/least suggestive of opioid withdrawal'.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Muscle spasm/twitching signals an **ADVANCED** opioid withdrawal state (scoring higher on the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale) - a distractor trap versus the more commonly recognised early features (lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, yawning, piloerection).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Penrose's Law/hypothesis specifically describes the **INVERSE** relationship between the number of psychiatric beds and the prison population — it is not a direct claim that mental illness causes crime, a subtly different (and wrong) paraphrase often offered as a distractor.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Forensics Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: There is explicitly **NO** reliable predictor for identifying which mothers will kill their children — despite recognised associations (teenage motherhood, affective disorder), the tested correct answer is 'there are no reliable predictors,' not one of the plausible risk factors offered as distractors.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Forensics Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Impulse control disorders are distinguished by demographic stereotype as much as by symptom: kleptomania (typically women in their 30s), pyromania (more often male adolescents with poor social skills/learning difficulties), trichotillomania and pathological gambling each carry a distinct typical profile — the exam expects you to match the vignette demographic, not just the behaviour.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/EMIs Forensic Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Stalking typology hinges on a subtle distinction: 'rejected' stalkers **HAD** a prior relationship and pursue reconciliation/vengeance, whereas 'intimacy seekers' had **NO** prior relationship but believe an imagined love will be reciprocated — both involve a hoped-for relationship, making them easy to conflate. Tested in both **SBA** and **EMI** formats.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Forensics Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Most exhibitionism offenders are aged 15–25, not middle-aged as intuition might suggest.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Forensics Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: The single best predictor of a **FUTURE** sexual offence is a history of **PREVIOUS** sexual offences — not the severity of the current offence or a specific diagnosis.

recurringTraps.text: **DSM-IV**'s (now-abolished) multiaxial system coded mental retardation on Axis 2 alongside personality disorder — a recall trap for anyone assuming Axis 1 (clinical disorders) is the more intuitive answer.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Learning Disability_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: **ICD-11** places dyslexia under 'developmental learning disorder' — easily confused with 'learning disability'/intellectual disability. The exam is testing that these terms are different diagnostic categories, not synonyms.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Learning Disability_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: A stem asks for the **FALSE** statement about schizophrenia in **LD**; the trap answer is 'thought disorder is probably more evident' — in reality thought disorder and complex persecutory delusions are **LESS** evident in severe **LD**, where unexplained aggression/bizarre behaviour dominate instead.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Learning Disability_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Challenging-behaviour criteria distinguish 'a few minutes' disruption at least **DAILY**' (which counts) from 'a few minutes' disruption on a **WEEKLY** basis' (which does **NOT** meet the threshold) — a single timeframe swap flips the correct answer.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Learning Disability_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: **PTSD** in **LD** presents atypically in children/adolescents: aggression (not nightmares or an exaggerated startle response) is the most commonly reported presenting symptom, reversing the 'classic' adult **PTSD** symptom profile candidates expect.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Learning Disability_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: In **ADULTS** with **LD**, an exaggerated startle response **IS** commonly reported (unlike some paediatric presentations) and symptoms are **NOT** reliably self-limiting within a few weeks — comorbidity with other psychiatric diagnoses is the norm, not the exception, and this is the opposite of what a 'quick recovery' distractor implies.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Learning Disability_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Attributable risk (a risk **DIFFERENCE**) can be negative when risk in the exposed is lower than the unexposed, but relative risk (a **RATIO**) can never be negative — and the odds ratio, not **RR** or **AR**, is the 'cross product' measure. Don't assume all these measures share the same numeric constraints.

Even a large, well-validated, randomly-sampled cross-sectional survey (e.g. a national comorbidity survey) can only ever estimate **PREVALENCE** — it can never yield an incidence rate, however good its diagnostic methodology.

Retrospective cohort studies need the **SAME** sample size as prospective cohort studies — the difference is purely the calendar timing of data collection and reliance on existing records, a frequently mis-answered 'advantage/disadvantage' question.
Prospective cohort studies do **NOT** cost less than case-control studies — this is a commonly tested 'which is **NOT** an advantage' distractor.

Stopping a trial early after an interim analysis shows a large apparent benefit tends to **OVERESTIMATE** the true treatment effect — this is a small-numbers/chance artefact, not evidence the intervention truly works even better than a completed trial would show.

A survey's response/completion rate is **NOT** the same statistic as a study's statistical power — a vignette quoting ==74%==/==60%==/==88%== response rates across groups is testing whether you know power cannot be inferred from response rate alone.

Meta-analysis pooling 12 uncontrolled trials + 3 RCTs: the trap answer is that mixing designs makes a meta-analysis impossible. Correct: it only weakens it — best practice is two separate meta-analyses.
Impact factor is tested as if it measures the quality of a specific article — it is actually a journal-level, 3-year rolling citation average.
When framing a **PICO** comparator for discussing a side effect with a patient, the trap distractor is an alternative drug; the correct comparator is 'not taking the intervention at all'.
Candidates over-trust the Cochrane Library as covering all trials — it maintains **CENTRAL** but not every intervention trial is registered there, and it is not a substitute for Medline.

**EMI** trap: distinguishing 'the prevalence of disease among test-positives' (= **PPV** = **TP**/total positive) from 'how likely a positive result is given disease' (= likelihood ratio, sensitivity/(1-specificity)) — these produce different-looking but easily confused fractions from the same 2x2 table.

source.file: question_bank/EBM/EMIs Evidence Based Medicine_ Attempt review.pdf

recurringTraps.text: Raising a diagnostic cut-off from 3 to 4 on the **CAGE** reduces sensitivity but leaves specificity **UNCHANGED** in the sourced worked example — candidates often assume specificity must rise whenever sensitivity falls.

In a positively skewed distribution, most **VALUES** fall to the **LEFT** of the mean (the mean itself is pulled right by a few extreme high values) — a commonly reversed detail; the 'tail', not the bulk of the data, is on the right.
"Odds for a ==90%== event rate" trips candidates who answer with the probability (0.9) or its complement (0.1) instead of computing odds = p/(1−p) = 0.9/0.1 = 9.

A one-tailed (rather than two-tailed) significance test for in-utero famine exposure and schizophrenia is justified specifically because the researchers already have strong prior grounds to expect the effect runs in **ONE** direction (exposure → illness, not the reverse) — not because of sample size, distribution shape, or number of control groups, which are the tempting-but-wrong distractors.

Recruiting fewer patients than the pre-calculated sample size (175 vs. planned 300) specifically raises the chance of a **TYPE** 2 error — the chance of type 1 error is **NOT** directly tied to sample size, a distinction the 'blue rabbit' worked example in the explanation makes explicit.

The p-value does **NOT** indicate the probability that the null hypothesis is **FALSE** (a very common misstatement) — it reflects the probability of the observed (or more extreme) data occurring **IF** the null hypothesis is true. The 'not correct' statement in this **SBA** is exactly this common misreading.

**EMI** vignette: a null **RCT** result contradicting strong prior belief/evidence after an adequately powered, rigorous 18-month trial is best labelled a **TYPE** 2 error possibility — not automatically 'the drug doesn't work' — while choosing sibling controls (who share genetic/parenting exposure with autistic probands) for a bonding study is **SELECTION** bias that would **UNDERESTIMATE**, not overestimate, the true association.

Cohort incidence-denominator trap: if 200 of an initial 1200 at-risk people already have the illness at baseline, the correct incidence denominator for new cases over the follow-up year is 1200-200=1000 (the truly at-risk group), not the original 1200.

Migrant schizophrenia incidence 3x natives but prevalence only 1.8x: the tested explanation is a shorter illness duration in migrants (via P=I x D) — but the explanation itself flags this as 'hypothetical and not a widely established explanation'. Plausible-sounding distractors like 'better access to care for natives' or 'better treatment response in natives' are wrong; know the intended answer even though it isn't settled science.

In P = I x D calculations, a stated mortality rate is often a deliberate red herring: prevalent ('existing') cases already exclude the dead by definition, so mortality figures given in the stem should be discarded rather than subtracted when solving for duration.

Two disorders with equal incidence but differing prevalence: the tested explanation is a difference in **CHRONICITY**/duration (P=I x D). The explanation explicitly downgrades competing distractors like differing stigma/awareness or sex distribution ('though A can be considered for a different class of disorders') — don't over-think this into a psychosocial explanation when a pure duration explanation is wanted.

Distinguishing epidemic/pandemic/hyperendemic/endemic/sporadic: 'pandemic' is specifically defined by wide **GEOGRAPHICAL** spread, not by size of case numbers, level above baseline, or fluctuation pattern (those describe epidemic, hyperendemic and sporadic respectively) — don't pick hyperendemic or sporadic as distractors for 'wide geographical distribution'.

Infant death rate is **NOT** an example of a standardized/adjusted rate — restricting a sample to a subgroup (here, age <1 year) is merely a specific rate. Only the standardized mortality ratio is genuinely adjusted for a variable (e.g. age) **AFTER** observation.
